name: Conchiglie
look: Medium conch-shaped shell, usually ridged outside, with a deep open cavity.
fact: The hollow works like a scoop: peas, bits of sausage and thick sauce get trapped inside, so each shell arrives pre-loaded.

name: Lumache
look: Short, fat curved tube pinched almost shut at one end, like a snail shell.
fact: One end is squeezed nearly closed, so sauce that flows in through the wide mouth has nowhere to go.

name: Lumaconi
look: Giant ridged snail shell with one wide opening, several centimetres across.
fact: Big enough to fill one at a time with a spoon or piping bag, then bake standing in sauce like a tray of little cups.

name: Pipe rigate
look: Ridged, bulging elbow with one wide open end and one flattened, nearly closed end.
fact: Named for the bowl of a smoking pipe. The flattened end acts as a stopper, turning each piece into a small sauce reservoir.

name: Pipette rigate
look: A small pipe rigate: a ridged curl about a centimetre long, closed at one end.
fact: The scaled-down pipe is a favourite for thick soups and for children, because every piece fits on a spoon with its filling of broth.

name: Chiocciole
look: Ridged, tightly curled short tube shaped like a garden-snail shell, open at both ends.
fact: Chiocciola is the Italian word for a land snail, and also what Italians call the @ sign.

name: Abissine
look: Small ridged shell with a rolled-in lip, a little like a tiny cowrie.
fact: One of several shapes named during Italy's colonial campaigns in East and North Africa in the early twentieth century; Abyssinia was the old name for Ethiopia.

name: Tofe
look: Plump, ridged shell curled nearly closed, rounder and deeper than conchiglie.
fact: Its deep, almost closed pocket holds more sauce than an ordinary shell, which is why it is favoured for chunky ragù and oven bakes.

name: Castellane
look: Ridged shell rolled lengthwise into a long, narrow scroll with a slit down one side.
fact: Introduced by Barilla in 1987. The company reportedly first called them paguri (hermit crabs) before settling on a name that evokes the long skirts of castle ladies.

name: Malloreddus
look: Small, plump ridged shell about 2 cm long, curled over on itself.
fact: Known as gnocchetti sardi, these striped Sardinian shells were traditionally rolled over wicker baskets and often tinted yellow with saffron.

name: Cavatelli
look: Small elongated curl of dough with a hollow down the middle, like a tiny hot-dog bun.
fact: Made by pressing fingertips into a small piece of dough and dragging it into a curl, one of the oldest pasta-making gestures and little changed since the Middle Ages.

name: Capunti
look: Open, elongated oval about 3 to 5 cm long with finger dents inside, like an empty pea pod.
fact: Each one is dragged across the board with three or four fingertips at once, leaving a row of dimples that catch sauce.

name: Strascinati
look: Flat, slightly curled oval a few centimetres long, rough on one side and smooth on the other.
fact: The name describes the method: a piece of dough is dragged across a wooden board with the fingers or a blade, so the board's grain roughens one face.

name: Cicatelli
look: Longish cavatelli-type curl hollowed with several fingers, the edges rolled inward.
fact: Typical of the Daunia hills of northern Puglia and neighbouring Irpinia, where they are also made with grano arso, flour from toasted wheat.

name: Raschiatelli
look: Long cavatelli, hollowed along their length with two to four fingers.
fact: The dough is 'scraped' along the board with the fingertips. In Basilicata and northern Calabria they are counted by how many fingers made them.

name: Cortecce
look: Elongated, rough-surfaced curl about 5 cm long with a furrowed hollow.
fact: A Campanian relative of cavatelli, dragged with three or four fingers so the piece curls like a strip of bark peeled from a branch.

name: Mischiglio
look: Dark, rustic cavatelli-like curls dragged by hand.
fact: A peasant pasta from the Pollino area of Basilicata, made from a mix of flours such as chickpea, fava bean, barley and durum wheat when wheat alone was too costly.

name: Foglie d'ulivo
look: Slim pointed leaf shape with a central crease, often tinted green with spinach.
fact: A Puglian shape that pays tribute to the region's olive groves; each leaf is dragged with a knife tip like a stretched orecchietta.

name: Parmatieddi
look: Large, flat cavatelli hollowed with four fingers into a long leaf-like shape.
fact: The Palm Sunday pasta of Teggiano in the Vallo di Diano: the shape recalls the palm or olive leaves blessed in church that morning.

name: Cruset
look: Small hollowed disc of dough pressed with the thumb, like a rough orecchietta.
fact: A mountain pasta of the Occitan-speaking Stura valley near Cuneo, proof that the dragged 'little ear' gesture is not only southern.

name: Skioufichta
look: Short, hand-rolled curls of dough a few centimetres long with a groove down the middle.
fact: A traditional Cretan pasta shaped by rolling small pieces of dough under the fingers, usually finished simply with hot oil or butter and grated cheese.

name: Makarounes
look: Small finger-pressed curls of flour-and-water dough, close cousins of cavatelli.
fact: The signature dish of the island of Karpathos, where the hand-rolled curls are topped with slowly browned onions and a local sharp cheese.

name: Orecchiette
look: Small domed disc about 2 cm across, thin in the centre with a thicker rim and a rough outer surface.
fact: In old Bari, women still sit outside their homes dragging small rounds of dough across wooden boards with a blunt knife, then flipping each one over the thumb.

name: Cencioni
look: Oval petal larger and flatter than orecchiette, slightly curved with one rough side.
fact: Named from cencio, a rag. The rough, curved petals are dragged like oversized orecchiette; in the Marche the same name is also used for a rustic noodle made with fava-bean flour.

name: Farfalle
look: Small rectangle with zigzag ends, pinched in the middle into a bow.
fact: Its name means butterflies, though many diners insist on bow ties. The pinched centre stays firmer than the thin wings.

name: Farfalloni
look: An oversized farfalla, with broad ruffled wings and a thick pinched centre.
fact: The larger wings make the contrast between soft edges and chewy centre even stronger than in standard farfalle.

name: Farfalle tonde
look: Bow tie with rounded, smooth-edged wings instead of zigzag-cut ones.
fact: Cut from an oval rather than a rectangle, so the wings come out rounded like a real butterfly's instead of pinked.

name: Strichetti
look: Hand-pinched bow of fresh egg pasta, softer and less regular than factory farfalle.
fact: The home-made ancestor of farfalle in Emilia: small rectangles of leftover egg sfoglia pinched in the middle, traditionally a way to use up scraps from making tortellini.

name: Sorprese
look: Small square folded corner to corner and pinched, like an empty tortellino.
fact: The 'surprise' is that there is no filling: the folded pocket is hollow, so it fills itself with sauce or broth instead.

name: Rotelle
look: Small spoked wheel with a ridged rim and a hub in the centre.
fact: A child of the machine age: spoked wheels can only be made with an industrial extrusion die. The gaps between the spokes trap sauce and small vegetables.

name: Fiori
look: Short extruded piece with a hub and curved petals, like a six-petalled flower or pinwheel.
fact: Essentially a wheel without its rim: the open petals give the sauce even more edges to cling to.

name: Quadrefiore
look: Short squarish piece with rows of ruffled fins, flower-like when seen from the end.
fact: A rare artisan shape extruded slowly through bronze dies; the stacked frills make it one of the most sauce-retentive short pastas.

name: Racchette
look: Small oval frame with a criss-cross lattice and a short handle, like a tennis racket.
fact: The open lattice does the job of a wheel's spokes, catching peas, diced vegetables and dressing, which makes it a pasta-salad favourite.

name: Dischi volanti
look: Small round disc with a raised rim and a dimpled centre.
fact: The name arrived with the flying-saucer craze of the mid-twentieth century; the dished centre holds a small pool of sauce.

name: Radiatori
look: Short, squat piece ringed with parallel ruffled fins around a curved core.
fact: It was inspired by industrial radiator fins in the twentieth century, and the fins do the same job: maximum surface area, here for holding sauce.

name: Creste di gallo
look: Curved tube like an elbow with a ruffled crest running along its outer edge.
fact: A hybrid design: the tube holds sauce inside while the frilled comb on its back grips sauce outside.

name: Campanelle
look: Cone of rolled pasta with a ruffled, flared edge, like a bellflower.
fact: Also sold as gigli, lilies, the flower on Florence's coat of arms. The hollow cone and frilled lip hold thick sauces well.

name: Mafalde corte
look: Short lengths of flat ribbon with ruffled edges on both sides.
fact: A bite-length cut of the long ribbon named for Princess Mafalda of Savoy; flat centre and frilly edges cook to two different textures.

name: Sagnarelli
look: Short, flat rectangular ribbons with zigzag fluted edges.
fact: Cut from a sheet with a fluted pastry wheel on all four sides, so every piece has a pinked border that holds on to sauce.

name: Trottole
look: A ribbon coiled into rings around a central stalk, like a child's spinning top.
fact: The curled ribbon forms a spiral channel that scoops up sauce, similar in effect to fusilli but more compact.

name: Vesuvio
look: Short coil of pasta wound into a lopsided cone, like a small volcano.
fact: A speciality of the pasta makers of Gragnano, near Naples, named for the volcano that dominates the bay.

name: Torchio
look: Flared, rolled cone open along one side, shaped like a torch.
fact: The wide flared mouth scoops up chunky sauces, working much like campanelle without the frilled edge.

name: Lanterne
look: Curved, deeply ridged piece of pasta arched like the ribbed shade of an old oil lantern.
fact: The deep ribs behave like the fins of radiatori, giving thick sauces plenty of grooves to settle in.

name: Cappellacci dei briganti
look: Small cone with a turned-up brim, like a pointed hat.
fact: Associated with Molise and southern Lazio, the shape imitates the conical hats worn by the brigands who roamed the southern Apennines in the nineteenth century.

name: Marille
look: Two parallel tubes joined side by side with a curling wing, ridged on the inside.
fact: Designed in 1983 for the Neapolitan maker Voiello by car designer Giorgetto Giugiaro. It won more press than sales and was soon discontinued.

name: Cascatelli
look: Short curved strip with two parallel ruffles standing up along one side, forming a trough.
fact: Launched in 2021 by podcaster Dan Pashman with the maker Sfoglini, after three years spent chasing a shape that holds sauce, stays on the fork and is satisfying to bite.

name: Spighe
look: Short piece patterned like a plaited ear of wheat, with a hollow along its length.
fact: A modern shape introduced by the Molise maker La Molisana in the 2010s as a tribute to the durum wheat the pasta is made from.

name: Andarinos
look: Small ridged spiral about 3 cm long, like a tiny hand-made fusillo with grooves.
fact: Made only in the village of Usini near Sassari: each piece is rolled by hand over a ridged board so it twists and takes on stripes at the same time.

name: Corzetti
look: Thin disc about 5 cm across, embossed with a different pattern on each face.
fact: These coin-like rounds from Liguria are pressed with carved wooden stamps, and older molds often carried aristocratic family crests or symbolic patterns.

name: Corzetti della Valpolcevera
look: Small figure-of-eight piece, pinched at both ends with the fingertips.
fact: The other Ligurian corzetti, from the Polcevera valley behind Genoa: no stamp is used, just a pull and a press of two fingers that leaves a little '8'.

name: Lorighittas
look: Thin strand looped twice and twisted into a small braided ring.
fact: From the Sardinian village of Morgongiori: a fine strand is wound twice around the fingers and twisted into a ring. Traditionally made for All Saints' Day, each takes about a minute by hand.

name: Su filindeu
look: Gauze-like sheet of hair-thin threads laid crosswise in three layers and dried.
fact: One of the rarest pastas in Italy, it is pulled and folded into 256 fine threads, dried as a woven sheet, then broken into broth for a Sardinian pilgrimage feast.

name: Lasagne
look: Wide, flat rectangular sheet of pasta, rolled thin.
fact: The plural name is traditional even when people mean one sheet. Sheet pasta is among the oldest forms: the word goes back to the Latin laganum.

name: Lasagne verdi
look: Flat egg-pasta sheet coloured deep green with spinach.
fact: In Bologna the classic baked lasagne is made with green sheets: spinach is worked into the egg dough, then layered with ragù, béchamel and Parmigiano.

name: Lasagne ricce
look: Long dried semolina sheet with wavy, ruffled edges.
fact: The dried, frilly-edged sheet of Naples' Carnival lasagna, layered with ragù, ricotta and tiny meatballs. It is also the model for the American 'lasagna noodle'.

name: Vincisgrassi
look: Thin egg-pasta sheet, in some recipes enriched with butter and a splash of vin cotto or Marsala.
fact: Legend says it was named for an Austrian general, Windisch-Graetz, at Ancona in 1799, but a similar 'princisgras' already appears in a Macerata cookbook of 1779.
pairings: giblet and meat ragù with béchamel

name: Sagne chine
look: Rustic sheet of semolina pasta for layering.
fact: Calabria's feast-day lasagna: 'chine' means filled, and the layers are packed with tiny meatballs, hard-boiled eggs, cheese and often peas or mushrooms.

name: Maltagliati
look: Irregular flat triangles and lozenges of thin egg pasta.
fact: The name means 'badly cut': they began as the uneven offcuts left when trimming a rolled sheet for tagliatelle, and imperfection is still the entire aesthetic.

name: Stracci
look: Large, irregular torn or roughly cut pieces of thin pasta sheet.
fact: A name used across central Italy for sheets cut or torn into ragged pieces, the quickest shape a cook can make from a rolled sfoglia.

name: Strapponi
look: Rough pieces ripped by hand from a rolled sheet, with ragged edges.
fact: No knife is involved: in Tuscany the cook tears pieces straight off the sheet and drops them into the pot, and the name comes from strappare, to rip.

name: Mandilli de sæa
look: Very large, almost translucent squares of pasta, served loosely folded.
fact: The Genoese name means silk handkerchiefs, and the sheets are rolled so thin that they drape and fold on the plate like cloth.

name: Testaroli
look: Spongy, pancake-like disc cut into diamonds about 5 cm across.
fact: From the Lunigiana: a thin batter is cooked on a hot terracotta or iron testo, cut into diamonds, then briefly soaked in hot water. Often described as one of Italy's oldest pastas.

name: Lasagne bastarde
look: Brownish, thick-cut squares or lozenges of pasta sheet.
fact: 'Bastard' because the dough of the Lunigiana hills mixes wheat flour with chestnut flour, which gives a faintly sweet taste and a darker colour.

name: Tacconi
look: Thick, roughly cut squares or short wide strips of sheet.
fact: In the Marche tacconi are traditionally made with a share of fava-bean flour, a habit from times when wheat had to be stretched with ground legumes.

name: Taccozze
look: Rustic diamonds or squares of thick flour-and-water sheet.
fact: An everyday pasta of Molise and neighbouring Abruzzo, cut into rough rhombuses and usually cooked together with beans or other legumes.

name: Blecs
look: Rough triangles or squares of dark buckwheat-flecked pasta.
fact: A Friulian mountain pasta made with buckwheat and wheat flour; the name is the local word for a patch of cloth.

name: Foiade
look: Broad, irregular lozenges or rectangles of fresh egg pasta.
fact: The rustic sheet pasta of the valleys around Bergamo, cut wide and uneven, and sometimes made with a little cornmeal in the dough.

name: Cresc' tajat
look: Rough, yellowish lozenges of thick sheet.
fact: A thrifty pasta from the northern Marche: leftover polenta is kneaded with wheat flour, rolled out and cut into diamonds.

name: Pantacce
look: Small dried lozenges with one or two ruffled edges, like chopped-up mafalde.
fact: Cut on the diagonal from frilly-edged ribbons, they recall the old habit of using up broken lasagne in soups.

name: Łazanki
look: Small squares or diamonds of rolled noodle dough, a couple of centimetres across.
fact: The name descends from lasagne; tradition credits the Italian-born queen Bona Sforza with bringing the idea to Poland in the 1500s. Also eaten in Belarus and Lithuania.

name: Fleckerl
look: Small flat squares of egg noodle about a centimetre across.
fact: A staple of old Habsburg kitchens: baked with ham as Schinkenfleckerl in Vienna, tossed with caramelised cabbage as Krautfleckerl, and known as flíčky to Czechs.

name: Csusza
look: Irregular torn pieces of thin egg noodle sheet, roughly 3 to 4 cm across.
fact: Traditionally torn by hand rather than cut. Its famous dish, túrós csusza, tops the hot noodles with curd cheese, sour cream and crisp bacon.
pairings: curd cheese, sour cream and bacon

name: Mlinci
look: Brittle, blistered sheets of baked dough, broken into pieces and softened in hot liquid.
fact: The thin dough is first baked dry, then broken up and soaked in hot water or roasting juices, so it sits between flatbread and pasta. Also made in Slovenia.

name: Andrajos
look: Torn, irregular scraps of thin flour-and-water dough, cooked in stew.
fact: A shepherds' dish from Jaén and neighbouring parts of south-eastern Spain: thin rounds of dough are torn into 'rags' straight into a stew of rabbit, hare or salt cod.

name: Pot pie noodles
look: Thick, soft squares of rolled egg noodle dough about 5 cm across.
fact: In Pennsylvania Dutch country 'pot pie' has no crust: it is a stew of chicken or ham in which large square noodles are simmered until slippery.
